name: Fluid Compartments, Plasma Osmolality, Starling Forces, and Hyponatremia

reference.source: Medical Biochemistry 5th ed / Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry 32nd ed
clinicalPearls: Total body water is 60% of weight: 2/3 intracellular, 1/3 extracellular (3/4 interstitial, 1/4 plasma volume)
Serum osmolality normally ranges from 275 to 295 mOsm/kg, calculated as 2*Na + Glucose/18 + BUN/2.8
Microvascular fluid flux depends on Starling forces: hydrostatic outward push versus albumin oncotic inward pull
SIADH presents with euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia, high urine osmolality (>100 mOsm/kg), and urine sodium >20-40 mEq/L
Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia (>8-10 mEq/L per 24 hours) causes fatal osmotic demyelination syndrome
reference.pathophysiology: Osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus regulate thirst and posterior pituitary ADH secretion to maintain plasma osmolality. In SIADH, unsuppressed ADH acts on renal principal cell V2 receptors to insert aquaporin-2 channels, reabsorbing free water and causing dilutional hyponatremia. When chronic hyponatremia is corrected too rapidly, water rapidly leaves brain astrocytes, precipitating oligodendroglial apoptosis and central pontine myelinolysis.
additionalDifferentials: Hypovolemic hyponatremia (dehydration, thiazide diuretics, cerebral salt wasting)
Hypervolemic hyponatremia (congestive heart failure, decompensated cirrhosis)
additionalInvestigations: Urine sodium concentration (distinguishes hypovolemic <20 from euvolemic/renal >40 mEq/L)
Serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glucose, and uric acid
Serum TSH and morning cortisol to exclude hypothyroidism and adrenal crisis as causes of euvolemic hyponatremia
